utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Good morning, everyone. Good morning, Mr. Hatchett.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Good morning, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. Good morning, Mr. Tieger. Please continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Good morning to you and Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Hatchett.

utterances.speaker: RONALD HATCHETT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Let me turn to the statement that you provided in written form and let me turn first to that portion of your statement which indicates that Dr. Karadzic told you during your visit that -- and as reflected in the interview you provided, that ethnic cleansing was not a Bosnian Serb policy but instead just a regrettable consequence of a civil war resulting from civilians who were extremist, intimidating or forcing out people of other ethnicities. I take it that you did not ask him specifically about in particular municipalities and specifically whether forces of the Republika Srpska Army or Republika Srpska police have been represented in those municipalities and that they had been doing in those municipalities at the time.

utterances.speaker: RONALD HATCHETT [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct, sir. I was primarily interested in what Dr. Karadzic's personal opinion was on these issues. I mean, it was obvious to anyone who was following what was going on at this time, that ethnic cleansing had been taking place on the part of all the parties. Croats cleansed Muslims, Muslims cleansed Croats, and Serbs cleansed Muslims and Croats and all. But my primary purpose here was to get a better insight as to Dr. Karadzic's positions on these things.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And were you aware then about evidence indicating the responsibility of organised forces of Republika Srpska, that is the VRS, the Army of Republika Srpska, or the Republika Srpska Ministry of Interior or police for the -- generally termed the ethnic cleansing of other ethnicities?

utterances.speaker: RONALD HATCHETT [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was not aware specifically of incidents where the regular Army of Republika Srpska was involved in ethnic cleansing at this time. This is in September of 1994. My impression was most of the ethnic cleansing was being done by these militia-type groups like Arkan's Tigers and other type of groups like that. I was not aware of the specifics of any incidents involving the regular troops of the Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I'm not going to go into a great deal of detail, but this Trial Chamber over the course of many months of trial has heard a great deal of evidence about events in municipalities and has heard evidence about the role of both the VRS and the Republika Srpska police in the -- in force exerted against other ethnic groups. So let me ask you quickly about just a few of those examples. The Chamber has heard evidence, for example, that in the Prijedor municipality in north-west Bosnia that in late May the military forces of Republika Srpska attacked a large Muslim settlement called Kozarac. Thousands of civilians were rounded up. Hundreds were killed, and there was massive destruction in the area as reflected in both eyewitness testimony and contemporaneous documents of the VRS that this Trial Chamber has received. Were you aware of that when you prepared your statement?

utterances.speaker: RONALD HATCHETT [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, sir, I was not aware of that. But again, what I would point out was I don't doubt that these kind of incidents took place, but as I said, the important thing that I was trying to elicit in my interviews with Dr. Karadzic is to what extent those incidents reflected the policies or the values of Dr. Karadzic. I don't doubt that there are those that have served and many have already been tried by this Tribunal, and the Tribunal has found evidence sufficient to convict them of these kind of things, but my question would be whether or not Dr. Karadzic had a role in causing those military actors to act in the way that they did.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I -- I trust you would agree, however, that it would be somewhat easier and more accurate to assess the reliability, credibility, or accuracy of any representations that Dr. Karadzic might make about that policy if you knew what the forces under his control had actually been doing in the municipalities; correct?

utterances.speaker: RONALD HATCHETT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, that's -- the assumption once again, that you just made, that is -- it was that those forces were under his control. My impression that I have --

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Okay. I want you to finish your answer, but I take it you would agree with the general premise of the point I made, that if you knew that --

utterances.speaker: RONALD HATCHETT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: -- it would help you assess.

utterances.speaker: RONALD HATCHETT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Okay. Now, please finish your answer.

utterances.speaker: RONALD HATCHETT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Now, what I was saying is that my impression from what I observed there was that there was not a very close working relationship between the political side of the Republika Srpska and the military side. My impression was that the military somehow believed that they were an entity unto themselves and they didn't necessarily have to -- to the extent that we are used to in the West, submit themselves to the control of the civilian authorities. So once again, you know, I would raise the issue of whether or not -- I can see a situation where Dr. Karadzic could have a certain view on these kind of activities and military commanders that theoretically were under his control but not actually, de facto under his control, would have a different point of view on those issues. So that -- that was again why I was focusing on what do you, Radovan Karadzic, think about this. I mean, I had this on videotape for two reasons. One, I was under contract at this time as an international affairs advisor to a television station in Houston which served an area of about 5 million homes, which was the fourth largest television coverage area in the United States, and I wanted to give them a chance to hear from supposedly the horse's mouth on what they -- what Dr. Karadzic believed about these things. So to get him on record saying the things that he had said, it would seem to me was a valuable way of letting the American people have a good idea about the nature of the man running the Serbian Republic at that time. And the other thing about this is I took these video-tapes and turned them over to my acquaintances in the Central Intelligence Agency, and it gave them a chance to judge for themselves, looking at his body language, the way in which he said certain things, to judge for themselves what his veracity was on these kinds of issues.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I take it in addition that Dr. Karadzic did not mention to you at that time, nor did you inquire specifically about events in the Zvornik municipality; is that right?

utterances.speaker: RONALD HATCHETT [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: So you weren't aware, as this Trial Chamber has received evidence, that after a long period of pressure, Republika Srpska military officials, military vehicles, tanks, took positions while RS officials told the Muslims of Kozluk that they had a very short time to gather themselves and leave and that transportation would be provided for that purpose, resulting in the expulsion of nearly 2.000 people. And I take it he didn't tell you that only a relatively few days later he, that is Dr. Karadzic, met with local officials in Zvornik who told him that, "We were most active in evicting the Muslims," and, "We have successfully implemented the President's decision to settle Divic and Kozluk with our children." And that can be found at P1478, pages 246 through 254. Is that correct, sir?

utterances.speaker: RONALD HATCHETT [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct. I was not aware of that, but once again I would just raise the issue of to what extent was this all initiated at the decision of the -- President Karadzic and to what extent was it carried out independently by the Serbian military.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I trust you would agree that had you had the information I just gave you that is before this Trial Chamber that might have assisted you in making [overlapping speakers] --

utterances.speaker: RONALD HATCHETT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, certainly. I would have asked a follow-up question then: How do you explain just -- what you just quoted me, but having no knowledge of it I didn't that follow-up.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Let me turn to some aspects of the proposal that he advanced to you. Among other things, he indicated that his proposal would include the fact that Bosnia would remain a single country; correct?

utterances.speaker: RONALD HATCHETT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And that's contained at paragraph 16 of your statement where you provide some of the details?

utterances.speaker: RONALD HATCHETT [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Were you aware that this was and had been throughout -- from before the war, throughout the course of the conflict during negotiations, a consistent position and demand by the international community?

utterances.speaker: RONALD HATCHETT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I was aware of that. It showed to me that he was willing to accept and incorporate into his concept of ending this many of the ideas. For example, the 49/51 split of territory was also something that was in the international community proposal of the Contact Group plan, whereas at this time, I think about 72 per cent of the territory of Bosnia was under the control of the Serbian military. And so he was saying, "I am willing to back away from this 72 per cent and go back to the 49 per cent as you have asked for in the Contact Group plan."

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Well, were you also aware that while Dr. Karadzic was acknowledging the position and demand of the international community, in this proposal he was also steadfastly maintaining to his subordinates and associates that the ultimate objective of Republika Srpska was unification with Serbia?

utterances.speaker: RONALD HATCHETT [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not aware that it was unification with Serbia proper. I am aware that he wanted a contiguous territory of Bosnia to be part of the Republika Srpska. I am aware that he wanted close ties with Serbs in the Krajina and that he wanted close ties with the Serbs inside of Serbia. As far as union, I was not aware of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Okay. So you weren't aware of such evidence as in -- as this Chamber has received as close to your discussion as the 9th much January, 1994, where he said, "Our goal is to unite with Serbia." That's P5525 at page 12. Or January 17th, 1994, where he said to the Assembly, "Our goal of unification is still valid." And that's P1387. Or when he responded later that year or at the beginning of 1995 when accused of squandering the chance to get a Greater Serbia, that "nothing has been squandered." Instead he explained that we're in a tug-of-war with the international community and the rope is on our side and every day we pull it one millimetre to our side. That's P1405, pages 148 through 149. You were not aware of that?

utterances.speaker: RONALD HATCHETT [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was not aware of the specifics that you just quoted, but once again, I would point out that what he had made and asked me to take to our governmental authorities was a proposal, and that proposal would necessarily involve compromise, which would have involved backing away from some of the positions maybe that he had established previously and accepting some of the positions that the international community had had in their proposals previously. And it also would have involved the international community accepting some new realities in the settlement that they had heretofore not accepted. For example, the main issue that I saw was that especially the United States had been pressing for a unitary state in Bosnia, that is with a single government in Sarajevo that would control the whole of the territory of Bosnia, whereas Dr. Karadzic's proposal was for a federal Republic of Bosnia, a single Bosnia, but with two constituent parts.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Doctor. And just by way of trying to make our discussion a little bit more efficient because I have limited time, I appreciate that the question involved the issue of negotiations generally, but I had simply been focused on the issue of the unification issue, so I'll ask you to just focus on the questions I ask and we'll either get there or Dr. Karadzic will have a chance to ask you questions in redirect. Only in the interests of time, sir.

utterances.speaker: RONALD HATCHETT [Resumed]
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Otherwise, I would be happy to invite an expansive discussion?

utterances.speaker: RONALD HATCHETT [Resumed]
utterances.text: I knew that there was discussion about unification of all of the Serbian peoples, just as there was discussion at this time by the Croats about unification of all the Croat peoples.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Okay. Now you had referred a moment ago to the amount of territory the Serbian forces held as being approximately 72 per cent. You refer to that in your statement as well and also refer to the characterization of the proposal that Dr. Karadzic made which included the 51/49 per cent split action generous. Now, would you agree that the generosity of such an offer would at least depend upon the -- who lived on the land that was under the control of the Republika Srpska forces before the war and how that territory was taken? That would have some effect on whether it was a generous offer or not?

utterances.speaker: RONALD HATCHETT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. But again if you look at the maps of the census prior to the war, about 60 per cent of the territory of Bosnia was identified as predominantly Serb in occupation.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Let me look quickly at the map that you provided. That's D2743, I believe. Can I take it that when looking at the eastern side of the country that those areas in green are supposed to be representation of Srebrenica, Gorazde, and Zepa?

utterances.speaker: RONALD HATCHETT [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Okay. And the rest of the territory in Eastern Bosnia is territory controlled by the forces of Republika Srpska?

utterances.speaker: RONALD HATCHETT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it's territory that Dr. Karadzic proposed be part of Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: RONALD HATCHETT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Excuse me. If I could point out, this is a map that I made after -- for presentations effects. The actual map that Dr. Karadzic gave me was a 1:250000 scale map which was much more accurate than what is depicted here, and it was that map that I gave to the American government that they used. I have moved about five times since this occurred and I could not locate the map, but the US government had copies of a map that was much more detailed than what we see in this exhibit here.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Okay. Dr. Karadzic was seeking that territory plus a trade for Srebrenica, Gorazde, and Zep. But do you know the demographic breakdown of Srebrenica and Gorazde?

utterances.speaker: RONALD HATCHETT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah. At this time these were heavily Muslim areas, but what he was trying to do was to avoid the islands of Muslims embedded inside of -- of Republika Srpska, because he assumed that those would -- those people would rather be part of the Bosnian Muslim Croat federation, and that's why the green that you see around Sarajevo was the territory that he was willing to trade where there was significant Serbian population. He was willing to trade that territory to the Muslims for the territories in those three enclaves in the east.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Did you know the demographic -- demographics of many of the other municipalities in Eastern Bosnia, in that area; Zvornik, Vlasenica, Bratunac, Visegrad, Rogatica, Foca? Did you know those before the war?

utterances.speaker: RONALD HATCHETT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I knew that.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And did you know that they were predominantly Muslim?

utterances.speaker: RONALD HATCHETT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I knew that. I knew that these existed.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And do you know what Dr. Karadzic said about why those municipalities came under the control of the Republika Srpska forces?

utterances.speaker: RONALD HATCHETT [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Well, he said the following in front of the Bosnian Serb Assembly. That's P00988. "To tell the truth, there are towns that we grabbed for ourselves and there were only 30 per cent. I can name as many of those as you want, but we cannot give up the towns we made up 70 per cent. Don't let this get around, but remember how many of us there were in Bratunac, how many in Srebrenica, how many in Visegrad, how much in Rogatica, how much in Vlasenica, in Zvornik, et cetera? Due to strategic importance they had to become ours, and no one is practically questioning it any more." Did he tell you that?

utterances.speaker: RONALD HATCHETT [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, sir, he didn't tell me that.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, did he -- now, did he also mention that he and other Bosnian Serb officials such as Momcilo Krajisnik had insisted that that area, the Eastern Bosnia area, the Podrinje area, had to be cleaned; that is, had to be Serbian?

utterances.speaker: RONALD HATCHETT [Resumed]
utterances.text: He wanted that territory to be part of Republika Srpska. That's what I understood. And it would have involved trading territories and which would imply movement of populations.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Okay. And did you know that from 19 -- from as early as 1992, that efforts had been undertaken and directives had been issued to achieve the removal of Muslim population from that area so it could be under Serb control?

utterances.speaker: RONALD HATCHETT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I knew that some Muslims had been taken from that area, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: But I'm -- I'm asking you if you were aware, as this Trial Chamber has heard evidence, that when -- that Dr. Karadzic not only acknowledged the objective of ensuring that this area was Serbian but had discussed that matter with his military forces and that directives and that orders were issued to achieve that by the military?

utterances.speaker: RONALD HATCHETT [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was not aware that Dr. Karadzic gave the orders to the military for that to occur.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: So you were not aware that as early as 8 November, 1992, Dr. Karadzic met with General Mladic and his corps commanders. That there was a discussion about which strategic objectives had been achieves. For example, the Posavina Corridor, and which had not, that is the cleansing of the Podrinje area or Drina area, that's P1481, at pages 146 through 147. And at that same month a directive was issued which provided that one of the corps of the Army of Republika Srpska had the responsibility to inflict the heaviest losses on the enemy forces in the wider Podrinje area and force them to leave the areas with the Muslim population. You weren't aware of that?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Excuse me, Mr. President. I think that in order to be fair, Mr. Tieger should alert the witness to whether that directive that he's referring to was something that was signed or authored by Dr. Karadzic, because he's presenting this as if Dr. Karadzic had done that, and in fact I think we know from the evidence that that's not the case.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Were you also aware that Dr. Karadzic had acknowledged in Assembly sessions that he, as had General Mladic, that he was aware of the directives, not to mention the fact that he was present at that November 8th session? Were you aware of that?

utterances.speaker: RONALD HATCHETT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I know that -- you know, he was in the midst of a war, and I know that he was a politician, and I know that a politician to stay in power has to appeal to his constituency, and my point simply is this: The fighting was going on. There were similar types of things that you just described the Serbs having done that were done to the Serbs by Muslims, by Croats, in territories that they were trying to make more ethnically pure as well. So this was being done in a three-way type of activity, and it is a tragedy, a real tragedy that this was going on. But my point simply is that he was bold enough to recognise that this can't go on, and he was -- and he made a proposal to try to end this kind of activity on the parts of all the parties by coming to a negotiated settlement. And if you take a look at what you proposed in September of 1994 and compare it to the Dayton plan that actually ended the fighting, then they're very similar. What happened was the US government and its Western Allies pocketed his proposal in September of 1994 and brought it out again in 1995 when the offensives by the Muslim armies weren't being as successful as they had hoped, but you know, what I'm saying is I'm not aware of a lot of things that were going on in the areas of the Croats and the Muslims either in terms of crimes against other ethnic groups.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Well, did Dr. Karadzic tell you during the course of these discussions and the proposal about which you some to be giving him a great deal of credit, that he'd been told and had reason to understand that the attainment of half of the territory or nearly half of the territory of Bosnia-Herzegovina would be a singular achievement, in fact a fairly unprecedented achievement, because of the ethnic cleansing that had taken place?

utterances.speaker: RONALD HATCHETT [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not sure I understand what you're saying.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Well, he related, for example, to the Assembly, that is Bosnian Serb parliament, how a British diplomat had told -- had asked him the other day why he wasn't acting triumphant, that in spite of the aggression, in spite of the ethnic cleansing, in spite of the atrocities, the crimes committed by your soldiers, that you are before the moment when the international community will recognise the results of your fight. Naturally you cannot get off the hook of 51/49 per cent, but how can you not realise that those 49 per cents are a great result and, as Dr. Karadzic said, a great victory of ours?

utterances.speaker: RONALD HATCHETT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, again, that sounds like a political statement. How can you say that if you started out with 60 per cent and you're now going to settle for 49 per cent that was a great victory. I think that was a political statement to try to put the best face on a proposal that he believed would ultimately solve the fighting that was going on in that region.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And he also told the Assembly that that was the first time in history that a country was torn apart after recognition and that the international community would accept it. By the way, those two cites are P1390, page 39, and P1385, pages 114 through 115.

utterances.speaker: RONALD HATCHETT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I would just say that 49/51 split is incorporated in the current situation in the country. So he was correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: By the way, just to clarify something that was raised by Mr. Robinson and which I also presume you're not aware of, and I wouldn't have asked you otherwise, this Trial Chamber in respect of the directive I read to you, this Trial Chamber's also received evidence that that directive was verbally approved by Dr. Karadzic. I take it that's -- you didn't know about the directive and you didn't know about his approval of it; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: RONALD HATCHETT [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And that's D2149 for purposes of the record. I think e-court page 13. Now, at the time you were talking to Dr. Karadzic, obviously Srebrenica and Gorazde and Zepa were still not under the full control of the Republika Srpska forces; correct?

utterances.speaker: RONALD HATCHETT [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And that's why you were seeking that trade?

utterances.speaker: RONALD HATCHETT [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Did he describe this to you as he did to the Assembly, that talking about the successful operations in 1992 and then saying, well, after that, that is after packing -- "Packing Muslims in small areas," or "thus achieving their concentration, we couldn't do more." Did he tell you that?

utterances.speaker: RONALD HATCHETT [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, he didn't tell me that.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: That's P988, pages 64 through 65. Now, were you aware at roughly the same time, that is in 1994, the Contact Group proposal had been -- was underway and had been advanced to the parties and was under -- had been under discussion?

utterances.speaker: RONALD HATCHETT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, of course. I was aware of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And I take it you were aware that the Contact Group proposal had not been accepted by Republika Srpska in part because it didn't provide for the territories that the Bosnian Serbs desired?

utterances.speaker: RONALD HATCHETT [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Do you know what Dr. Karadzic said about what would happen or what should happen if the Contact Group proposal was not accepted?

utterances.speaker: RONALD HATCHETT [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Okay. Well, at P1394, in roughly the middle part of 1994, he said, "We have to --" if that plan was not accepted, "We have to prepare ourselves according to the wish of our enemy. Be ready for -- to make intensive life-and-death war 'until his complete defeat or until our defeat and expulsion from these territories.'" And he went on to say, "In case of his victory, our enemy would not be generous nor merciful but merciless and ready for our extinction. Therefore, if we do not accept the plan, we have to accept the logic of our enemy and defeat him mercilessly leaving the mercy after the victory." You didn't discuss that with Dr. Karadzic, I take it.

utterances.speaker: RONALD HATCHETT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I did. You know, once again, this is a wartime situation. This is a politician talking to other politicians and to his constituencies. All I know is that I personally observed Dr. Karadzic becoming very short, if not irate, when General Tolimir kept pushing and pushing in the discussions we were having one evening for us -- for me in particular to agree as a military man that the best solution the Serbs could hope for was a military victory by overrunning Sarajevo. And Dr. Karadzic, as I said, almost in anger cut him off, saying listen, I am not going to agree for an all-out attack on a major populated area like this with the intendant loss of life that would occur on all sides when we know we're not going to be able to keep that territory in a negotiated outcome. So you know, this was a private, without the politicians around, without a constituency around, this was a private meeting of military and top leadership and the visitors.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: A private meeting with a visitor or more visitors from the United States present?

utterances.speaker: RONALD HATCHETT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, with me present, one other American present -- no, two other Americans present, and two British.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Well, you've just told me about the quote I read you from Dr. Karadzic about being merciless in attaining the objectives that you considered that that might be only a political statement, but are you aware of fact that some months later Dr. Karadzic issued and signed a document known as Directive 7, which included the language: "By planned and well-thought out combat operations, create an unbearable situation of total insecurity with no hope of further survival or life for the inhabitants of Srebrenica or Zepa." Were you aware of that?

utterances.speaker: RONALD HATCHETT [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not aware of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you. Now as a final matter I'd like to turn to the issue of what Dr. Karadzic told you about the -- what would happen at the end of the war and the supposed obligation as he considered it of all three republics, to enable the refugees who wished to come back to their homes to do so. First of all, were you aware of the fact that Dr. Karadzic often spoke of the demographic threat presented by Muslims, that is that they had a high birth rate and would overwhelm the -- the Serbs were at risk of being demographically overrun by Muslims.

utterances.speaker: RONALD HATCHETT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. And I knew that that was the concern of many Serbs and also of the Croats, because -- and that's why both the Serbs and the Croats initially opposed the idea of a unitary state in Bosnia, because they knew that that meant inevitably domination by a Muslim portion of the population, which already had the plurality and would move to a majority very quickly.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: We discussed earlier the rejection of the Contact Group proposal. Were you aware that one of the objections by the Bosnian Serbs to the Contact Group proposal was the fact that it provided that there would be no border controls on the borders between the entities and therefore for freedom of movement of goods, services, and persons throughout the union? That was considered a problem as -- by the Bosnian Serbs?

utterances.speaker: RONALD HATCHETT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I knew that the Bosnian Serbs wanted control of the borders of their entity, but that's as far as I knew.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Right. Within the country. So that would mean that they would be able to control not only the movement of goods and services but the movement of Muslims or Croats into the Serbian entity; correct?

utterances.speaker: RONALD HATCHETT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Theoretically, yes, that would be correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And were you aware that Dr. Karadzic, since 1992, had been -- that is since the issue of possible constituent units within Bosnia-Herzegovina had been discussed, have been stressing the need for those borders, that the borders of the Serbian entity, the Bosnian Serb entity, to be as wide, to be as big, and as thick as possible; that is, to be as impenetrable as possible. Were you aware of that?

utterances.speaker: RONALD HATCHETT [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not sure I understand what you mean by that.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Well, this Court has received evidence that Dr. Karadzic had said about the Bosnian Serbs entity that the -- that the -- having -- that the external borders of Bosnia and Herzegovina would not be a problem because they would strive to make the borders of the Bosnian Serb entity as wide as possible, that is to have as big an entity as possible, and to have them as thick as possible, that is to make them as -- to have as much control over who came in as they could?

utterances.speaker: RONALD HATCHETT [Resumed]
utterances.text: All I know is that he was willing to settle for 49 per cent of the territory, and as long as he was given control over the borders of that territory. That's what I knew.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And those references are at D88 and D456 for the benefit of the Court. Now --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second, Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Please continue, Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And finally, Mr. Hatchett, I wanted to ask you if you were aware that -- because you talked about Dr. Karadzic's acknowledgement of the requirements about the international community or the conditions demanded by the international community, if you were aware of his explanation of the need to give the impression that the Bosnian Serbs agreed with the right of return as well as an explanation of how to frustrate that right of return?

utterances.speaker: RONALD HATCHETT [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not aware of anything like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Well, this Trial Chamber has received evidence that Dr. Karadzic discussed that on more than one occasion. So on one occasion in 1994, that's in -- that's P1385 at pages 126 through 127, when one of the officials said, "What I would really like to see here is a firm attitude that the Muslims and Croats will not be allowed to return to the areas under our rule." Dr. Karadzic explained that they would not be in a position to ban the return of refugees and in principle all refugees could return, but that he would therefore add one sentence to the proposal, "This also has to be a two-way process." And that means that the Muslims, for example, from Prijedor, could only return to Prijedor if the Serbs now in Zvornik return to Zenica. And he discussed that again at P13 -- at P988, at page 29, when the same issue was raised about the right of return, and he said: "That's our intention, to say all right, everyone has the right to return to his home after the war if that is an overall process. What does that mean, an overall process? That means that the Muslims from Kozluk can return to Kozluk if the Serbs from Kozluk return to Zenica. If they don't want to return -- if they cannot return, then we need a new war to exchange that, and that's why I think we should always insist on this. So an overall process, either overall or none at all. We can act the Serbian Cyrillic way and tell it to their face or we can be a bit cunning. We do have to be a bit cunning." Were you aware that while Dr. Karadzic was acknowledging to you the right of return that he was discussing ways to frustrate them?

utterances.speaker: RONALD HATCHETT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, that's your interpretation of what that meant, but my interpretation of it is that he was saying that it has -- the policies have to be the same for all peoples. If the Muslims are going to have the right to return to their homes inside of Serbian territory, then Serbs also have to have the right to return to their homes inside the territory of the Muslims or the Croats. That's an interpretation that I think is equally valid.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: All right. And you find that to be --

utterances.speaker: RONALD HATCHETT [Resumed]
utterances.text: You find that to be logical.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And you find that to be cunning as well; is that right?

utterances.speaker: RONALD HATCHETT [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I find it to be logical.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: No, but Dr. -- I'll leave it at that, Mr. Hatchett. Thank you for responding to my questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I have nothing further, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you.
