utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. I would now like to read the summary of General Hayes's statement in English. [In English] General Vere Hayes is a retired officer of the British Armed Forces. From April to October 1993, he served as Chief of Staff of the United Nations Command for Bosnia and Herzegovina. He held the rank of brigadier. On April the 8th, 1993, just two days after his arrival, he was made aware of an incident in which the Bosnian Serbs discovered ammunition hidden in the truck of one humanitarian organisation, shipment of humanitarian relief which was being transported from Sarajevo airport to Bosnian Muslim-held area of Butmir. I deliberately didn't mention the name of this organisation. A total of 24 boxes of 9. -- 7.9 millimetre ammunition and a similar number of boxes of 12-millimetre ammunition were found hidden between the containers and drop bed of the trailer. This organisation found an additional 24 boxes of 7.9 millimetres and 12-millimetre ammunition hidden in the same place in another trailer at Sarajevo airport. Brigadier Hayes had no information to suggest that UNPROFOR or these other humanitarian organisation personnel were complicit in the smuggling of the ammunition. However, he realized that unfortunate incidents such as this provided the VRS with a reason to be cautious in inspecting humanitarian convoys of this organisation in the future before allowing them to pass. One of the most pressing issues upon his arrive was the fighting in Srebrenica. This was the focus of many meetings and negotiations over the first month of the stay of General Hayes in Bosnia. On April the 17th, 1993, General Hayes attended marathon negotiations at the Sarajevo airport concerning the cessation of hostilities in and around Srebrenica. At approximately 2.00 a.m. on 18th of April, 1993, an agreement for the demilitarisation of Srebrenica was signed. The agreement called for a total cease-fire in the Srebrenica area and deployment of an UNPROFOR company into Srebrenica and the evacuation of seriously wounded and ill persons by air. It was further agreed that the demilitarisation of Srebrenica would be completed within 72 hours of the arrival of the UNPROFOR company. All weapons, ammunition, mines, explosives, and combat supplies, except medicine, inside Srebrenica were to be handed over to the UNPROFOR. No armed persons or units would remain within the city once the demilitarisation process was completed. Neither side was to hinder the freedom of movement and humanitarian aid would continue to be allowed into the city as planned. It was further greed that a working group would be established to work on the -- to work out the detailed implementation of the demilitarisation. Brigadier Hayes was given the task within the UNPROFOR of leading these efforts. One of the details which was left to the working group was to delineate the geographical boundaries of the safe area that was to be demilitarised. This was a major stumbling-block between the parties. At a meeting of -- on 20th of April, 1993, it was finally agreed that despite their different positions on the delineation of the safe area, the city itself would be part of it and would be demilitarised. On 20th of April, 1993, Brigadier Hayes wrote out an operational order under which to implement the agreement. He defined the demilitarised area as urban area of Srebrenica itself, as well as the hills immediately overlooking the urban area from which a direct line of sight into the town existed. On 21st of April, 1993, Brigadier Hayes travelled to Srebrenica by helicopter with a delegation of the Bosnian Muslim and Bosnian Serb representatives. The purpose was to confirm that the demilitarisation had occurred, to agree upon the boundaries of the demilitarised area, and to physically mark the area. When they arrived in Srebrenica, they went in an armoured personnel carrier to the weapons collections -- collection area. When Brigadier Hayes alighted, he encountered Naser Oric, the commander of the BiH forces in Srebrenica. Oric was armed, as were his two bodyguards. Brigadier Hayes talked to Oric for about half an hour and explained the agreement to him. Brigadier Hayes explained to him that if he remained there when the Serbs appeared, the agreement would not be implemented since he was armed in the demilitarised zone. When Brigadier Hayes got the Serbs out of the APC, Oric was gone. The Serb and Muslim representatives inspected the weapons collection area, toured the boundaries of what Brigadier Hayes had proposed as the demilitarised area of the city and the overlooking hills, and went to the PTT building where they signed the notes reflecting the demilitarisation agreement. The agreed-upon boundaries never extended beyond the urban area and the location on the hills immediately overlooking it that gave a direct line of fire into the city. On May 17 -- the 17th, 1993, Brigadier Hayes attended a funeral for civilian victims of a Bosnian Muslim attack on the Serb villages -- village of Ratkovici. The bodies of the victims of the July 1992 attack had been exhumed from a mass grave. In early August 1993, the Bosnian government threatened to withdraw from the Geneva peace talks unless the Serbs pulled back from the positions they had taken on Mount Igman and Mount Bjelasnica around Sarajevo. Dr. Karadzic returned from Geneva to try to resolve this situation. Brigadier Hayes attended a meeting on the 5th of August, 1993, in Pale with the Bosnian Serb leadership, including Dr. Karadzic. This was the first time he met Dr. Karadzic. He found him to be perfectly civil and reasonable. Dr. Karadzic proposed that Serb forces withdraw from Mount Bjelasnica and Mount Igman as demanded by President Izetbegovic as a precondition for rejoining the talks in Geneva. He said that Serb forces would be willing to withdraw so long as UNPROFOR would ensure that the army -- BH Army did not occupy the area vacated by the Serbs. Karadzic accepted General Briquemont's suggestion that UNPROFOR monitor the area after Briquemont explained that UNPROFOR did not have sufficient troops to occupy the area. Dr. Karadzic also proposed opening a route between Zenica and Sarajevo and agreed to General Briquemont's suggestion that the route from Mostar to Sarajevo through Hadzici also be opened. Dr. Karadzic agreed to the establishment of a joint commission to ensure the restoration of utilities and infrastructure in Sarajevo. After the meeting with Dr. Karadzic, the VRS entered into a written agreement to withdraw their forces from Mount Igman and Mount Bjelasnica. Brigadier Hayes participated in negotiations leading to this agreement. The Serbs fully complied with the agreement for the withdrawal of their troops from Mount Igman and Mount Bjelasnica. That would be the summary.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: General Hayes, there's one issue that I would like your assistance in clarifying since you were the author of a map. Can we call up 1D6304. You were behind the initiative to draft the map.

utterances.speaker: VERE HAYES
utterances.text: Yes, I did draft the map, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: In this document, the map can be found on page 9.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can it be magnified. Can it be also placed -- can it flipped so that we have it in the north-south direction and we can read the letters. Counterclockwise. Thank you. Perhaps this will be fine.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: General, can you please explain to the Chamber what this map depicts?

utterances.speaker: VERE HAYES
utterances.text: I can. If might be simpler if I was able to draw, draw it diagrammatically. I'm afraid I'm not an artist, but I will do my best.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. Could you wait until assisted by our usher, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Certainly, sir. Would it be possible to have a blank screen so I could draw a diagram?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Or you can write on it as well. If you'd like to have a blank --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: My thoughts are is it might be easier to understand if I just draw a diagram on a blank screen. I think if I draw on this map we will -- we will not necessarily be able to -- to understand it as easily.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well, that can be done. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: In the meantime, Mr. President, we wanted to tender this document with the map. So can that be done before we leave this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We may come back to this document after having heard his explanation because we haven't heard anything about this document yet.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Is this screen okay?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, it should be coming.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Okay. The difficulty in establishing what would be an agreed safe area was that neither side could come to any compromise about it. And eventually having looked at the proposals of both sides and listened for a considerable length of time to them, I decided myself that if we just do this -- let's put -- north is up there. This is the road from Zvornik. And there is a road that goes out to Zepa at the bottom. I decided that they had both agreed within what they said, that the urban area of Srebrenica itself, no matter what they proposed, was within the agreement. So that's where the town itself was. I further decided that if that was to be a safe area, then it was important that the area that was drawn included certain points - I will symbolise them with triangles, which is a military symbol to signify an observation post - on the high ground that gave direct line of sight into the city. And I then drew the line of the safe area to encompass the buildings of the town itself and these high points. The line of confrontation was out here diagrammatically. So you had the Serbs on one side and the Muslims were inside. This area here was the only area that was a safe area. Between that boundary and the confrontation line was not within the safe area agreement. No armed person was allowed to stay within this area that I have hatched, and no weapons were allowed to be held within that area. But that did not apply to this area between the limit and the confrontation line. I hope I have explained that, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: So why don't we put some annotation for the future use. Could you --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Certainly, sir, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Could you indicate the urban area with a -- yes. That's --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Confrontation line.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: That's the confrontation line, yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I always find it very hard to write on these screens, I'm afraid.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: That's okay. And the safe area.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: What's happening here?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: You can delete as well, if necessary. Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It's not very tidy, I'm afraid.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Shall we keep it and give the number for the next Defence exhibit.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: It shall be assigned Exhibit D2756. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Should a date be placed and General Hayes' initials?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, point's taken. We saved it already. Shall we upload it again, then?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. We can note who -- who drew this picture, so it's not necessary. Let's continue, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Can we look at 1D6304 again. Can we have page 9 again.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: General Hayes, is this an accurate map? Does it depict the town proper, as it were, and the hills overlooking the town?

utterances.speaker: VERE HAYES
utterances.text: As far as I can tell from that, sir, it's the map that we drew, and that will be the one that we signed as part of the agreement, so it would be accurate.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Was it foreseen that the other safe area, that of Zepa, should be together with this particular area or were they two separate area?

utterances.speaker: VERE HAYES
utterances.text: It was intended that if Zepa was made a safe area, it would be a separate safe area.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Who controlled the other areas -- or, rather, does this safe area coincide with the boundaries of the municipality of Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: VERE HAYES
utterances.text: No, it does not coincide with the boundaries of the -- of the Srebrenica municipality. I'm not sure who was controlling the areas. All I can say is that between the area that is marked as a safe area and the confrontation lines, on the inside, if you wish, the side nearest the safe area of the confrontation line, would have been in the hands of the BiH, and outside those areas, to the best of my knowledge, would have been controlled by the VRS.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. One more question. What was the situation like when it came to the shelling of the safe area at the time you -- you were there after the signing of the agreement?

utterances.speaker: VERE HAYES
utterances.text: After the agreement had been signed and we had taken both sides' delegations in, we had marked the area on the map, we had marked it on the ground, and we had visited it. To the best of my knowledge, there was no firing, or there was no shell-fire received in that safe area during the rest of my time in Bosnia-Herzegovina; that is, up until the middle of October, 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you, General, sir.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can this document be admitted into evidence, please?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Ms. Edgerton.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: No objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Could we see page 5 of this document. Page 6, next page. General, do you remember whose handwriting this is?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I cannot remember the names of it, but they -- these were written by the representatives of the two delegations that came in, the BiH representative and the VRS representative.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Can we see the next page. Who signed on behalf of behalf UNPROFOR.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The UNPROFOR representative there is Colonel Geburt, G-e-b-u-r-t. He was the lieutenant-colonel in command of the 2nd Battalion of the Canadians, CanBat 2 is the way to which it was referred. He was the senior officer of the Canadian detachment which was a company-plus strength that went into Srebrenica to oversee the demilitarisation and put observation posts around the safe area.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Do you remember who signed for Bosnian Serbs and for Bosnians.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I can't remember their names, sir, but the names are on the front of that document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you. We'll admit it.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: It shall be assigned Exhibit D2757. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Please continue.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. For the time being I have no further questions for General Hayes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Before you begin, it's better to have a break given the time. Mr. Hayes, we'll have a break for half an hour and resume at 7 minutes past 11.00.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Very good, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Robinson.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. If I could just take a moment to introduce our legal intern who is present with us during this session. Her name is Romina Arnaudova from Bulgaria. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. If I could just take a moment before Ms. Edgerton commences. With respect to the redactions in the statement of -- that was previously discussed just before we adjourned, the transcript, as I understand it appears to identify paragraphs 2 through 15, although Dr. Karadzic himself had mentioned 2 through 16 which appeared to embrace the Focatrans incident. We also noted that that discussion continues in paragraphs 18 through 20. I wanted to bring that to the Court's attention in case the court considered that paragraphs 16 and 18 through 20 also fell within the parameters of the Court's concern.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We'll take a look and come back to the issue. Yes, Ms. Edgerton.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Good morning, Brigadier Hayes.

utterances.speaker: VERE HAYES
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: I would generally like to ask you some questions about the conversation that we had the day before yesterday, but before doing that, perhaps you could just confirm to me that your job with UNPROFOR was to be the principal staff officer at BH command headquarters in Kiseljak; correct?

utterances.speaker: VERE HAYES
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: So Kiseljak is where you were based and operated from.

utterances.speaker: VERE HAYES
utterances.text: That's correct, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And Kiseljak is about 25 kilometres from Sarajevo. Is that correct as well?

utterances.speaker: VERE HAYES
utterances.text: Correct, through three Serb check-points.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And to travel into Sarajevo -- or you said yesterday that you travelled into Sarajevo often to the airport -- pardon me, the day before yesterday, to the airport for negotiations, occasionally to the PTT building or the residency, but that you weren't in the city of Sarajevo proper - those were the words we used - very often.

utterances.speaker: VERE HAYES
utterances.text: That's correct. I travelled in to see the commander in the forward headquarters, to see the French commander of Sector Sarajevo in the PTT building but mainly to the airport for negotiations and Mixed Military Working Group meetings.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And keeping that in mind, I asked you the day before yesterday about your impressions of Sarajevo, and you told me a few things, and I'd like to run through those to see if I've understood your impressions correctly. Among other things, you said that you had the feeling that normality had broken down a bit. Is that so?

utterances.speaker: VERE HAYES
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And that was, among other things, because you saw a lot of dogs running around and they were eating dead dogs.

utterances.speaker: VERE HAYES
utterances.text: That's one incident that particularly stuck in my mind.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: You also mentioned seeing lots of devastation and damaged buildings.

utterances.speaker: VERE HAYES
utterances.text: That's correct, yeah.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: You noted that people would not go out very often.

utterances.speaker: VERE HAYES
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And you recalled having seen barricades of containers, cars, and other things at exposed areas and intersections. Is that also correct?

utterances.speaker: VERE HAYES
utterances.text: That's correct. Mainly on the eastern side as we drove in from the south going north towards the residency. They were beyond the eastern side.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: In the context of a discussion about the airport crossings and how they were, in your view, a function of the desperation of people in Sarajevo, you also talked about it being difficult for people to get food and ordinary commodities and noted that they didn't want to go out because of the dangers. Do I have that right?

utterances.speaker: VERE HAYES
utterances.text: Yes. People did cross the airport out of -- or attempt to cross the airport out of desperation to leave Sarajevo, although it was -- any movement across the airfield was banned, as I understood it, in the agreement that had been drawn up between the United Nations and the Serbs for the use of the airport, but, yes, people did attempt to move out. And the normal commodities that you would expect in a city were in short supply, including water.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: I asked you the day before yesterday whether and what kind of a briefing you had received on the situation in Sarajevo on assuming your duties, and you advised that there was almost no time for a real hand-over from your predecessor because of the situation in Srebrenica at that time. Correct?

utterances.speaker: VERE HAYES
utterances.text: That's correct. I was required to move to assume the post of Chief of Staff a week earlier than was expected because my predecessor left to go to Vicenza, and so we didn't have a hand-over at the time that I was actually assuming the appointment. We had meet before for a short period, but again with so much going on, there was little time for much discussion.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And, in fact, you said the day before yesterday that the shelling of Sarajevo was not at that point at the top of the agenda because of the situation in Srebrenica. It was, if you like, a fact of life. Do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: VERE HAYES
utterances.text: Certainly the situation in Sarajevo was not something that I was dealing with at that time, although my first meeting with President Izetbegovic was to discuss the possibility, amongst other things, of getting the sewage system repaired. So it was not completely forgotten about, but the situation in Srebrenica was the more important one to try to resolve at that time.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: All right. Now, just moving on to the incident referred to in paragraphs 5 to 8 of your statement on April 8, 1993, involving the discovery of ammunition in an aid shipment at Butmir. You had no personal involvement in that matter, did you?

utterances.speaker: VERE HAYES
utterances.text: No. I was notified of it, but it depends what you mean by no personal involvement.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Were you called to go on scene? Were you involved in any investigation of the incident?

utterances.speaker: VERE HAYES
utterances.text: No. I was involved in no investigation of the incident, and I was not called to go and look at what had occurred.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: So your involvement or knowledge of the incident was limited to your being notified?

utterances.speaker: VERE HAYES
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now, in regard to that incident you said at paragraph 8 of your statement that you realised that unfortunate incidents such as this provided the VRS with reason to be cautious in expecting convoys in the future before allowing them to pass. Now, we also talked about this the day before yesterday, and perhaps I could tell you what I understood you to be saying in regard to that passage, and tell me if I've understood you correctly. You explain that we should take this to mean that you could understand why the Serbs became quite difficult at check-points, but while you could understand it, it doesn't necessarily excuse the fact that Serb forces would hold convoys for up to three days?

utterances.speaker: VERE HAYES
utterances.text: That's correct. I can fully understand why they became difficult. There was paranoia that UNPROFOR was not acting in a way that they expected or anticipated. They believed that we would smuggle in ammunition to Sarajevo and to other Muslim enclaves, and they also believed that humanitarian aid organisations would do the same. And so an incident such as this was -- was grist to that particular mill. So that was a bit of a complicated explanation. It was -- it fed their paranoia, I'm afraid, but just it didn't -- it did not justify holding convoys for three days, but then quite often that was because of the arguments that occurred between the convoy commander demanding freedom of movement and the Serb check-points insisting that they inspected it. So there was an immediate clash which often took a long time to resolve and perhaps somebody else like a United Nations military observer would have to go along to try to mediate.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And just in regard to this incident before we leave it altogether, it's correct, isn't it, that UNPROFOR never established -- was never able to establish how that ammunition was placed in that shipment?

utterances.speaker: VERE HAYES
utterances.text: To the best of my knowledge, that's correct. I was not involved in any further investigation, and I cannot remember anything coming across my desk in relation to it apart from that piece of paper that you already have seen.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And were you aware that -- no. Actually, I'll move on. Moving on in time in terms of the chronology of events you discussed in your statement to 11 April 1993, can you confirm that Srebrenica was shelled on that day?

utterances.speaker: VERE HAYES
utterances.text: I can't confirm it. I mean, I can look in my -- in my diary if that's permissible.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: By all means.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Srebrenica was being -- was being shelled, and it was one of the main reasons why it was at the top of the list of priorities.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And this diary you're looking at, is that a contemporaneous diary you recorded during your tour?

utterances.speaker: VERE HAYES
utterances.text: It is. It's one that I kept for my own purposes. It's not very comprehensive, I'm afraid. I think the only thing I can say about it, from my diary, is to say that there is an entry which says that the parties agreed to attend if there was no more shelling. I must take that to mean that General Halilovic agreed to attend if there was no more shelling. From that, I have to conclude that there may have been shelling on that day. Certainly one incident of shelling in which some children were, sadly, killed gave rise to a press report of body parts being found on the wire being surrounding the area where I think they had been playing. I think it was a school. That was the catalyst, really, for getting the situation in Srebrenica up to the top of the agenda.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now, this incident that you've just discussed, did that incident to your recollection take place on the 12th of April?

utterances.speaker: VERE HAYES
utterances.text: I can't remember. I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: All right. Perhaps I could show you something that might help your recollection. 65 ter number 13346. It's a letter from the UNPROFOR Force Commander, Lieutenant-General Wahlgren, to Dr. Karadzic on the situation in Srebrenica, dated 12 April 1993.

utterances.speaker: VERE HAYES
utterances.text: I see it, yeah. There's an information copy that has gone to myself in Bosnia-Herzegovina command, main headquarters in Kiseljak. So I will have seen that, though I cannot recollect it at the moment.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Could we go over, if you've had a chance to look at this first page, to the second page of this document. And perhaps we could magnify it a bit. Now, this letter from General Wahlgren to Dr. Karadzic refers to, at paragraph A, the latest casualty estimate in Srebrenica being 35 dead and 68 wounded, but those are only the ones that have approached the hospital. And at paragraph B, this quotes a report from his people in Srebrenica. Paragraph B notes that the report says: "I have personally seen and counted 14 dead, including 7 bodies on the road in front of the schoolhouse used as a refugee centre where it appears most casualties occurred. Two of the seven bodies I saw in front of the hospital were children, and one has been -- or one was decapitated." Does this sound like the incident you just referred to, Brigadier?

utterances.speaker: VERE HAYES
utterances.text: Yes, it does. In paragraph A, though, the latest casualty estimate in Srebrenica will refer, in my opinion, to the number of casualties over a period, and not the number of casualties necessarily that will have occurred as a result of any shelling on the 11th. Similarly in paragraph B where -- it would be a United Nations military observer who is submitting this report, I think. In paragraph B he says: "I personally have seen and counted 14 dead, including 7 bodies ..." Again, that does not mean, in my opinion, that that is the result of shelling on the 11th. I think those are figures of shelling over a number of days rather than on a particular day. I suspect that the last sentence in paragraph B is the incident to which I -- to which I'm referring where he sees -- he reports bodies in front of the hospital being children.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you. Could we have this as a Prosecution Exhibit, please, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: No objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, that will be admitted.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: It shall be assigned Exhibit P6077. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now, could we just have still on the subject of the 12th of April, 1993, a look at 65 ter number 24415, which is a BH command Kiseljak, and I say this by its cover sheet, a BH command Kiseljak G3 operations report on the same meeting you refer to in paragraph 10 of your statement? And before we go further into the document, maybe you want to just have a look at paragraph 10 to refresh your memory. And we can certainly collapse the B/C/S version of this document.

utterances.speaker: VERE HAYES
utterances.text: Okay. I have read that, and in my diary there is -- I would take from my diary that I did not attend that meeting. I went to the airport but then moved on to do some other work elsewhere.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: All right. Thank you. Now, G3 main Kiseljak -- G3 BH command main Kiseljak would have come under your command. Is that the case?

utterances.speaker: VERE HAYES
utterances.text: Sorry, G3 plans.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: VERE HAYES
utterances.text: Yes. G3 plans was a staff branch which was under my command.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: So this is a report. Can we -- can we take from this and as well from the hand-written notations at the bottom left-hand corner of the cover sheet where we see, among other things, COS, that this is a report that would have come across your desk?

utterances.speaker: VERE HAYES
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, if we can go to -- slowly through the document --

utterances.speaker: VERE HAYES
utterances.text: Is it possible to see what that report says? I may -- what the rest of that -- I've only seen the cover sheet so far.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Absolutely. I've just asked for us to go slowly through that document to give you an opportunity.

utterances.speaker: VERE HAYES
utterances.text: Sorry. I thought you were referring to a different document.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: No, no, not at all. And when you've had a chance to skim this, please let us know so that we can move on to the next page.

utterances.speaker: VERE HAYES
utterances.text: Yes, I've read that. All right. I've read that page. Yeah, read. Read.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And there should be one more page -- oh, pardon me. There should be one more page of relevance with the attendees at this meeting, General Wahlgren, Mr. Thornberry, General Morillon, Mr. Mendiluce, Ms. Boyd, General Mladic, General Gvero, General Tolimir, and Major Indic. Now that you've had a look at this, Brigadier, I wonder if we can go back to page 3 of this document at paragraph 6. Now, in paragraph 6, we see about halfway through that first main paragraph General Mladic say, among other things: "The complete truth was that Srebrenica was not attacked and that it was completely quiet in the area." Which actually quite sharply contrasts with the information you had and the reports we've just seen about shelling in Srebrenica on the 11th and 12th of April, doesn't it?

utterances.speaker: VERE HAYES
utterances.text: Did we have a report of shelling on the 12th of April? I thought it was on the 11th.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: That was the document we just finished, and I refer to the document that we just finished discussing, which was the letter of protest from General Wahlgren to Dr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: VERE HAYES
utterances.text: Was that dated the 12th? Sorry, we'll just go back to it. There are sometimes a problem between the date of the document as its transmitted and the information that it is actually containing as a report. I apologise if I missed it.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Oh, not at all. P6077 was the number. Formerly 65 ter -- you have it. Thank you very much. You see the cover page of the document --

utterances.speaker: VERE HAYES
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: -- is date --

utterances.speaker: VERE HAYES
utterances.text: Yup, it's dated the 12th of April.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you. And if you go to the next page of the report itself, I note that --

utterances.speaker: VERE HAYES
utterances.text: Yeah. I suspect that this is a report that has come from a United Nations military observer on the 11th and has been forwarded by the force commander on the 12th. So I suspect that that -- what he's reporting there is what happened on the 11th, and things -- it was always very difficult, but I suspect that what General Mladic is saying on the 12th is that it's quiet now. He would pick his words very carefully. Sometimes things were lost in translation, but I believe he would be -- he was saying it's quiet on the 12th. And looking at that, I would -- I would think that it is reporting shelling on the 11th, not on the 12th. Though I can't do more than say that's my interpretation of it.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you. I'll move on then. Now, I would actually like to go in your statement all the way over to paragraph 41 and the associated news article you refer to in this paragraph which you commented on, and in this news article, which is dated 4 August 1993, you're reported as saying: "There is still a military siege, but there has never been a humanitarian strangulation --"

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Shall we upload that document. Exhibit D2754.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Oh, pardon me, yes, of course.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: 2754. Exhibit D2754. Or 1D5526.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now, you're reported as saying: "There's still a military siege, but there has never been a humanitarian strangulation of Sarajevo." Now, in that regard I actually wanted to ask you whether you can confirm that we discussed this remark the day before yesterday, and you indicated you would like to actually temporarily limit your remark to your period of service in BiH and no time before or after that. Do I have that correct?

utterances.speaker: VERE HAYES
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now, during our meeting, you also said that aid came into Sarajevo via the Kiseljak route and the air-lift.

utterances.speaker: VERE HAYES
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And at the end of July, beginning of August 1993, you said that aid to Sarajevo was actually blocked by fighting in central Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: VERE HAYES
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now, I'd like to turn to 65 ter number 01227, which is the third periodic report on the situation of human rights in the territory of the former Yugoslavia submitted by Mr. Mazowiecki, who was the Special Rapporteur of the commission of human rights -- on human rights, and it's dated 26 August 1993. And he reports on the situation in terms of humanitarian aid in the area at that time. If we could go over to paragraph 14 on page 3 under the heading "Blocking of Humanitarian Aid." Now, in that paragraph he says -- he refers to 430.000 people are estimated as being dependent on food aid in Sarajevo and its surrounding areas and says that the main supplier is the United Nations high commission for humanitarian -- or pardon me, for refugees, UNHCR. And if we could go over to the next page, paragraph 15, he reads -- he states -- reports that convoys, UNHCR convoys which provide food and fuel for Muslims, Croats, and Serbs alike in Sarajevo have been obstructed or attacked by Bosnian Serb, Bosnian Croat forces, and sometimes also by government forces. He refers to a July -- July 1st, 1993, incident where Bosnian Serb authorities introduce taxes on all aid convoys crossing their territory, stopping deliveries for five days, until which point UNHCR was declared exempt. He refers to a 12-day delay on the 10th of July when Bosnian Croat authorities refused to issue aid convoys with permits to enter territory under their control, and also in paragraph 16, talks about recent attacks on convoys. In July 1993, he says nine UNHCR fuel trucks were blocked at Blazuj, which is outside Sarajevo, by over 100 heavily armed Bosnian Serb soldiers with a tank and other armoured vehicles, and the fuel from four trucks was confiscated before the convoy was allowed to pass ten hours later. He also refers to a UN aeroplane involved in relief flights having been hit six times since 21 July by fire from positions held by the government of Bosnia and Herzegovina. Now, looking at this, it seems that Mr. Mazowiecki's report paints a situation somewhat more dire than your remarks on the 4th of August, 1993, suggests, doesn't is?

utterances.speaker: VERE HAYES
utterances.text: What I said has to be taken in the context of what was happening at that time. When those remarks were made, the Geneva peace conference was underway, and it was in danger of stalling because of the fighting up on Mount Igman and Mount Bjelasnica, and because of this depiction of a siege of Sarajevo. I discussed what was actually happening at that time with Mr. Thornberry, and the problem, as is indicated in paragraph 14 of this, was a fuel convoy. At that particular time, the main problem for Sarajevo was getting in sufficient fuel, and the fuel convoy was being blocked in Central Bosnia by the fighting between the Muslims and the Croats. That is what was stopping the aid coming up through Central Bosnia into Sarajevo. The air-lift was continuing, and my remarks were focused on that in particular. Certainly there was difficulty getting aid into Sarajevo, but it did continue to come in, and it fed. It fed the citizens of Sarajevo of all three ethnic types, and understandably it also fed the government forces, the BiH, who were in there, as you would expect, because there was -- there was no other source of food apart from the black market. I hope that puts it into context for you.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Your indulgence for a moment, Your Honours. Thank you very much, Brigadier, I have nothing further.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you, Ms. Edgerton. Yes, Mr. Karadzic, do you have re-examination?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Sir, you were shown a letter that General Wahlgren sent to me. Do you know what my position was as regards Srebrenica after the 12th of April until the 8th of May when the agreement on demilitarisation was signed?

utterances.speaker: VERE HAYES
utterances.text: I'm not quite certain I understand the question, sir. Are you talking about the -- referring to your attitude as to what should happen as regards the fighting around Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Yes. Do you remember? Do you know how operations around Srebrenica were aborted, how they were stopped?

utterances.speaker: VERE HAYES
utterances.text: I understand from looking at that message that you sent that you directed your forces under commander General Mladic to cease operations there. I don't recall seeing it at the time, but I do understand from seeing that particular message that you gave the orders for General Mladic to cease operations there.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Taking into account what you know about Srebrenica, about Igman and Bjelasnica, what was your experience in addressing me as regards military matters? How did I react to the United Nations' requests? Were my responses positive or negative to those requests?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Edgerton. Before you against, General.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: I wonder if this is actually a matter that was raise the in cross-examination, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Will you move on to another topic, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Well, in that case I don't have any more questions. All that remains for me to do is thank the general for his testimony.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Unless my colleagues have a question for you, Mr. Hatchett, that concludes your evidence. On behalf of the Chamber, I would like to thank you for your coming to The Hague to give it.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Now you're free to go.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you, sir.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And just a slip of the tongue, Your Honour. This is Mr. Brigadier Hayes, not Mr. Hatchett.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: My apology, Mr. Hayes. My apologies. We are hearing so many witnesses.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Not a problem, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. President, the next witness is a protected witness and will require some protective measures as well as some other persons to enter the Chamber, so it may be wise to take a short break to accomplish that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. We'll do so. You may leave, Mr. Hayes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: The Chamber will now issue two oral rulings, first on the admission of MFI P6072, a press report dated 27th of December, 1994, which was used by the Prosecution on the 15th of January, 2013, during the cross-examination of Witness Milosav Gagovic. The Chamber reiterates its consistent practice that any third party statement not prepared for the purpose of criminal proceedings may only be admitted if they are commented upon, confirmed, or adopted by the witness on the stand. In relation to MFI P6072, Gagovic testified that the portion of the article read to him "refers to that same event," as that referred to in an earlier part of his testimony. The Chamber is therefore satisfied that, contrary to the circumstances surrounding 65 ter 45111C which admission was denied on 5th December and confirmed on the 11th of December 2012. In this instance, Gagovic has sufficiently commented on those portions of MFI P6072 which were read out to him on the 15th of January, 2013, for the purpose of admission. The Chamber shall therefore admit it into evidence the three paragraphs of MFI P6072, starting with the questions: "How did you arm the people? You did that right in front of the enemy, under sniper rifle? And it was probably Gagovic." The remainder of MFI P6072 shall not be admitted into evidence. Next, the Chamber will issue an oral ruling on the accused's request for presence of counsel to Witness Dragomir Milosevic, filed on the 15th of January, 2013. In the motion, the accused notes that the witness is scheduled to commence his testimony in these proceedings on the 22nd of January, 2013, that the registrar has assigned an attorney to him in connection with this testimony, and that the witness would wish to have his attorney present in court during his testimony. On the 15th of January, 2013, the Office of the Prosecutor stated that it did not wish to respond to the request. The Chamber has no issue with the witness's attorney, Mr. Stephane Bourgon, being present during the witness testimony and therefore grants the request. On a similar issue on the motion for modification of order for the temporary transfer of General Galic filed on the 14th of January, 2013, the accused states that the dates of Mr. Galic's transfer to the UNDU should be postponed due to the scheduling of conflicts of Mr. Galic's attorney. The motion states that Mr. Galic's attorney is to be present during his proofing and testimony. So therefore, Mr. Robinson, could you confirm that this is in fact a request that Mr. Galic's attorney be present in court?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: And I take it there's no position from the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: The Chamber grants the request. And unless there's a problem from the parties, on the part of the parties, the Chamber is minded to have an hour break today and adjourn at 3.00 instead of 2.45. Would there be any problem?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: No, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: None.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Would five minutes be sufficient for the change of setting?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: I believe so, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. The Chamber will rise for five minutes. --- Break taken at 11.55 a.m.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Would the witness take the solemn declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Please be seated.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I take it you understand you are referred to as KW571 instead of your real name.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Your face and your voice will not be heard or be seen by the public. Do you also understand that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I do indeed. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Witness KW571.

utterances.speaker: KW571
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like to call up 1D7011 [as interpreted] in e-court, and it shouldn't be broadcast. 1D7100.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation].

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Witness, could you please take a look the document in front of you and tell us whether this is indeed your name on it?

utterances.speaker: KW571
utterances.text: Yes, that is my name.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] [no interpretation].

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We'll admit it under seal.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: It shall be assigned Exhibit D2758, admitted under seal. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Witness, we sent a questionnaire by the Defence team, and did you answer the questions in it?

utterances.speaker: KW571
utterances.text: Yes, I did, sir.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like to call up 1D05914, also not to be broadcast.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Is this the first page as the cover page of your answers to the questionnaire that was sent to you? We have it both in French and in English.

utterances.speaker: KW571
utterances.text: Yes. That is indeed the document I received.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second. Could the Chamber move into private session briefly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Karadzic, please continue.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Can pages 2 and 3 of the document be shown, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Not broadcasting.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Certainly.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Is that page 1 of the answers to the questions?

utterances.speaker: KW571
utterances.text: Yes, indeed.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we show page 2 for the witness, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Is that the second page of your answers?

utterances.speaker: KW571
utterances.text: Yes, this is page number 2, indeed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. If I were to put these same questions to you now, would your answers be the same as the ones provided here in the document?

utterances.speaker: KW571
utterances.text: Yes, sir. My answers would be the same.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can I tender the document into evidence under seal?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Any objection, Ms. Edgerton?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. We'll admit it.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: It shall be assigned Exhibit D2759 under seal. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: French translation seems to be overlapped with English, but could you repeat, Ms. Edgerton.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: I actually don't get any French translation on my microphone, so I'm glad to have had the opportunity to raise that. I would like to ask for private session to raise the point I'd like to make if I may, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Could the Chamber move into private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're back in open session, Your Honours. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. As you have noted, Mr. Witness, Mr. Karadzic has completed his examination-in-chief, and your evidence was in most part admitted into evidence in writing. Now you'll be further asked by the representative of the Office of the Prosecutor in its cross-examination. Yes, Ms. Edgerton. Do you have any questions?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: I will, Your Honours, but I recall Your Honours' scheduling for today, and I wonder if --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Oh, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: -- this is the time you had marked for the break or I'm in Your Honours' hands.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We will have a break for one hour and resume at 1.30.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Edgerton.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. If I may, I think I would like to begin the cross-examination in private session for the reasons I indicated earlier for a very brief period of time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're in open session, Your Honours. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Now, in -- Mr. Witness, in your written evidence, in your answer to questions 5 and 6, still on translation issues, you used the term "entonnoir." Did you use that term to describe the mortar's crater?

utterances.speaker: KW571
utterances.text: Indeed. The word "entonnoir" is used in the military jargon in French because it's the shape that is formed by the shell. But indeed from a generic point of view, this means the crater itself.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And in your answers to question 8 and 9 in the same document, you refer to something called "puits de fusee." Is this a term used to describe the tunnel created by the mortar's fuse, the fuse tunnel?

utterances.speaker: KW571
utterances.text: The fuse tunnel is not created by the shell but by the fuse itself from the projectile, which when exploding moves ahead of the rest and is going to create a tunnel. This is why it's called a fuse tunnel or a detonator tunnel.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And is that what you mean to describe when you use the term "puits de fusee"?

utterances.speaker: KW571
utterances.text: Yes, Madam Prosecutor, indeed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, your training with your national forces was within the Engineers Unit and focused on the safe extraction and disposal of unexploded ordnances; correct?

utterances.speaker: KW571
utterances.text: Indeed, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And, in fact, although you continue to work in that field, you don't claim to have any ballistics expertise or specialisation in the area of ballistics. You're not here as a ballistics expert; correct?

utterances.speaker: KW571
utterances.text: No, not as an expert in ballistics.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Now, the training you had -- oh, pardon me?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. President, I didn't object. It was a compound question there, and I'm not sure that the answer actually was complete, so I was wondering if maybe she can rephrase that or break it up.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We can continue.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Fine. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: In terms of your training with your national forces, crater analysis was actually not a part of that programme, was it?

utterances.speaker: KW571
utterances.text: At the time in question, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And you were only concerned with the soil or terrain in which an ordnance was located to the extent it affected your main mission, the safe removal of ordnances. Isn't that so?

utterances.speaker: KW571
utterances.text: Yes, indeed. The objective was to remove safely the areas by removing unexploded ordnance.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And the first time you were involved in crater analysis training was when you joined UNPROFOR and arrived in the former Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: KW571
utterances.text: Yes, indeed, Madam Prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And how long was that training?

utterances.speaker: KW571
utterances.text: Two days. One to two days.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And the crater analysis that you carried out at the market-place in Sarajevo was your first and only official investigation of that type during your tour; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: KW571
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Just one more question about your written evidence. In your answers to questions 5 and 6, you discuss generally about how tail fins are embedded in craters, and I wonder if I could ask you have you also seen situations where mortar tail fins are not located embedded in the craters, they're found elsewhere?

utterances.speaker: KW571
utterances.text: During our tour, indeed we found other mortar craters where tail fins were embedded, but we also found other craters without any tail fins. Now, given that the areas were not very safe, we did not go beyond the crater to see whether we would find tail fins and check that it did correspond to mortar shells.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Now, specific to the investigation in question, I just want to ask you about your methodology on one area only. That's the methodology you used in determining the direction of fire. Was that methodology something you learned in the two-day training programme you underwent?

utterances.speaker: KW571
utterances.text: Yes, indeed. This is a methodology that was taught and showed to us by the person in charge of training and during the two days and that we attended this course.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: In terms of the crater itself, if it had been caused by a device, a static -- that generated a static explosion, how would that crater have been different in shape from the crater you saw?

utterances.speaker: KW571
utterances.text: If we are dealing with a static explosion device, in fact, if there is fragmentation that is linked to the explosive, it will be spread in the uniform manner around the load that's on the ground. On top of it on the ground you will have traces of powder of explosive that are going to blacken the area around the impact, whereas in fact on -- as far as this crater is concerned, the shape of it leads us to believe that the shell came following a curve, and therefore the projection was regular all around the shell that hit the ground. So the projection is regular and does not match what would look -- what it would look like if it was a static explosion, because, in other words, we would find the shape of the mortar if this mortar had been just placed on the ground, which was not the case here.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now. I think you've answered all my questions. Nothing further, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well, Ms. Edgerton. Mr. Karadzic, do you have any re-examination?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just two brief questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, you have been asked whether this was your first and last crater analysis. Have you received any official rejection of your analysis? Did any of your superiors dispute it?

utterances.speaker: KW571
utterances.text: No, not as far as I know.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You were also asked about the appearance of the crater. I should like to know when there is enough time and opportunity to drive the stabiliser into the ground with a hammer?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Perhaps Dr. Karadzic could rephrase.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Do you follow, Mr. Karadzic?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Could you distinguish between a stabiliser that followed a fuse after an explosion and a stabiliser that was driven into the ground by a hammer?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: I -- pardon me. I don't think that arises from cross-examination, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Agreed. I agree, Ms. Edgerton.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Witness, is of any relevance to the -- the extraction of the stabiliser and the trimming of the crater, is it of any relevance if we want to establish the facts?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Again. Yes, Ms. Edgerton.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
