utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: It's difficult to see how it arises from Ms. Edgerton's cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Esteemed Ms. Edgerton asked about the crater and its appearance, when a shell explodes on the ground as opposed to a shell that landed. I'm asking whether the same effect may be achieved by different means. Can it appear to be the same? If you do not allow this question, no problem.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I'm not sure she raised that. I think she referred to static explosion. If you could assist me, Ms. Edgerton.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Pardon me. Yes, I'm just trying to locate it quickly in the transcript. My question was: "In terms of the crater itself, if it had been caused by a device, a static -- that generated a static explosion, how would that crater been different in shape from the crater you saw?"

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: It's different from hammering the crater into the ground. Please move on, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Then I wanted to express my gratitude to the witness for coming here to testify.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Then, Mr. Witness, that concludes your evidence. On behalf of this Chamber I thank you for coming to The Hague to give it. Now you're free to go. But just one matter, Mr. Robinson, before Mr. Witness goes away. The Chamber is still seized of your motion to subpoena this witness. I take it that's now moot and you are ready to withdraw it.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. We withdraw it and thank the witness and the state for their co-operation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Shall we draw the curtain so that the witness can be excused.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I take it the next witness is also a protected one.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: That's correct, Mr. President. And there's also a representative to accompany this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. President, I've been negligent once again to identify our intern who is present in court during this session, and I saw you looking at me, but I was wondering what I did wrong. I forgot to worry about the intern. So anyway, we're pleased to have Claire Markwell from Durham university who is part of our team and she's joined us during this session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Ms. West will be taking my chair, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: While we are waiting for the next witness, the Chamber will give its ruling about Mr. Pljevaljcic's statement. In relation to the statement of Trifko Pljevaljcic, the Chamber held earlier today that paragraphs 2 to 15 be redacted from his statement. The Prosecution then submitted that paragraphs 16 as well as 18 to 20 also fell within the parameters of the Chamber's order. The Chamber has further reviewed Pljevaljcic's statement in light of the Prosecution's submissions. The Chamber first notes that the English translation of the paragraphs added after the proofing session is poor and at times incomprehensible. The Chamber considers that paragraphs 18 to 20, indeed, refer to the pre-war Focatrans incident in relation to which the accused, as himself stated, that too much importance has been given and which should therefore be redacted from the statement in line with the Chamber's earlier order. Paragraph 16, however, mostly relates to April 1992 and does not fall within the purview of the Chamber's order. In light of the fact that only five short paragraphs would remain in Pljevaljcic's statement after redaction, i.e., paragraphs 1, 16, 17, 21, and 22, and that the English translation of the newly added paragraphs is problematic, the Chamber considers it in the interests of justice that the witness be led live and only on those issues which are relevant to this issue -- to this case. As stated earlier this morning, should the accused wish to ask a question as to the Focatrans incident, the Chamber will decide at the appropriate time whether the question can be posed upon hearing the objection from the Prosecution. You can bring in the next witness. Good afternoon, Ms. West.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. President. Good afternoon Your Honours and everyone in and around the courtroom. There is one brief matter to address. We can do it in the presence of the witness and his lawyers. It regards paragraph 30 of the statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. I was wondering if we could do that in public session, but I'm now assured we can, Ms. West.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Would the witness take the solemn declaration, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: My apologies for interrupting.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. Please be seated and make yourself comfortable.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I see three members of the representative from Canada.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Two members. Welcome Mr. Fox and Ms. Soliman. Yes, Ms. West, before we hear the evidence of the witness.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. If I can direct your attention to paragraph 30 of the statement, and in paragraph 30 the witness indicates an activity that he was involved in once he returned from Bosnia on his first tour in July 1995 and before he returned back to the region in December of 1995. During that period of time, he tells us that he reviewed what he describes as highly classified intelligence information concerning the events in Srebrenica. He says that he was seeking to determine if there was any information that the accused had been involved or informed about the executions that had taken place after the fall of Srebrenica. He then tells us that he found no such information, and he found it significant because given the level of information he reviewed, had the accused been involved or been informed of the execution, this witness would have expected it to be reflected in those materials. Mr. President, we asked Defence counsel whether they themselves had access to those materials or had seen those materials, and they informed us -- we asked on January 7th. They informed us on the same date that they did not have the material referred to in paragraph 30, nor had they seen it. On this same day, we asked the Canadian government whether we could see that material as well, and on January 9th, we were advised the witness did not have the material referred to in paragraph 30 and that he was drawing on his memory. They also advised that if we wanted to see the material, we would have to make a formal request for it, but they noted that doing so would take some time to process. That was on January 9th. We declined to start that process, quite candidly, Mr. President, because understanding how much time it would actually take would only delay this witness. And further, if this material indeed was highly classified information, the possibility of actually ever receiving that material, I suspect, would be rather low. However, we are now still left with this paragraph, and I now would ask for the paragraph to be excluded from the statement, and my reason is that it is the Prosecution's position that it would be unfair to allow the admission of this paragraph as we wouldn't have any ability to fairly or thoroughly cross-examine exactly what this witness relied upon when he made this very significant statement. Secondly, this would be particularly difficult considering that we understand that the witness referred -- or reviewed this material in the fall of 1995, which would have been at a time when the witness hadn't been given any advantage or perspective that we now have because of the passage of time, and even if he had seen a document that would have connected the accused to the events, he may not have been aware of it because he was so close to the events. And it's for those reasons that I would ask that paragraph 30 be excluded.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Could you expand a bit further as to the point that this paragraph should be deleted instead of going to a matter of weight at the end of the day?

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm fully confident that the Court could make that appropriate consideration, but the significance of the statement he makes in this paragraph is quite bold, and without the materials that he's reviewed, I am at a loss as how to handle any cross-examination regarding it, and it's for those reasons that I'd ask that you exclude it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Can I hear from you, Mr. Robinson.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. Besides the issue of weight which we feel is quite correct, the Prosecution has had this statement since September 2012 and could have easily made inquiries, requests for binding orders, if necessary, and would likely have been successful in at least having the material identified and if -- if such material was identified, you could be in a position to decide whether or not to disclose it to them. But to raise it on the day of the cross-examination I don't think warrants the remedy of exclusion. So you can give it whatever weight you wish. They can cross-examine to the extent that they can, and even after this testimony, if they still wanted to make a binding order request, they can do that, and if it's necessary, we can have the witness back.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I add something from my amateurish position or layman's position. On several occasions we heard hearsay evidence from the evidence. This is much more reliable than any hearsay. We did not insist on them bringing the source of the hearsay to this courtroom. We accepted what they presented to us.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Would you like to add anything, Ms. West?

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: No thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Ms. West, the Chamber is of the view that all this goes to the issue of weight, so we will not exclude the paragraph at the moment. Yes, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Witness.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like to call up 1D7101 in e-court, and the document shouldn't be broadcast.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Witness, what you see in front of you on the screen next to the number KW554, do you see your name and your date of birth, and are both correct?

utterances.speaker: KW554
utterances.text: Yes, I do, and they are both correct.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. I would like to tender this document into evidence under seal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: It shall be assigned Exhibit D2760 and it's under seal. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And now I would like to call up another document which shouldn't be broadcast, although it might be, as a matter of fact. 1D06001. If you believe that it may be broadcast, we would not object to that.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. President, the last page with the signature shouldn't be broadcast.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Witness, did you provide a statement to my Defence team?

utterances.speaker: KW554
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Would that be the statement that you see in front of you on the screen?

utterances.speaker: KW554
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Does your statement truly reflect your words?

utterances.speaker: KW554
utterances.text: Yes, it does.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. If I were to put the same questions to you here today, would your answers be the same as they are in this statement?

utterances.speaker: KW554
utterances.text: Yes, they would be.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you sign the statement?

utterances.speaker: KW554
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we display the last page now, but that page should not be broadcast.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Is this your signature, sir?

utterances.speaker: KW554
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. I would like to tender this statement into evidence pursuant to Rule 92 ter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Robinson, are you minded to tender a public redacted version of this statement, redacting the signature part?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. We'll do that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. Any objection, Ms. West?

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I take it there are no associated exhibits.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. We'll admit both versions.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Statement shall be assigned Exhibit D2761, admitted under seal, and the public redacted version shall be admitted as Defence Exhibit D2762. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Please continue, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. I don't have any questions for this witness, at least for the time being.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: For the public benefit -- benefit of the public, are you going to read out the summary?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, yes, Excellency. I apologise. I'm going to read the summary in English, and I don't think that there are any reasons for this to be read out in private session. [In English] Witness KW554 was an intelligence officer for the UNPROFOR in Zagreb. During his time in UNPROFOR, it was a widely held belief among Western-oriented intelligence analysts, including himself, that the Bosnian Muslims were responsible for some of the notorious shelling incidents which had killed and wounded many people in Sarajevo. It was believed that the Muslims were shelling their own civilians in order to blame the Serbs and obtain foreign intervention in the war on their side. It was widely believed that United Nations forces -- within the United Nations forces that at least one of the market-place shellings in Sarajevo was caused by the Muslims. On one occasion when discussing the responsibility of the Muslims for the first Markale Market place shelling which had occurred before he arrived in the former Yugoslavia, a US soldier confirmed that the Muslims were responsible for this shelling and displayed that he said -- what he said was a photograph of a person dropping a mortar shell from window overlooking the market -- Markale Market place. Concerning the second shelling of the Markale Marketplace, the Witness KW554 was informed that the round had been recorded on a Cymbeline radar but it could not be determined from which side of the confrontation line it had been fired. He received credible information that the Muslim -- Bosnian Muslims were violating the Sarajevo weapons exclusion zone in May 1995. However, it was well known that NATO would never launch air-strikes against the Bosnian Muslims because the Muslims had the political support of the United States. During the time of Witness KW554 in Bosnia, there were personnel on the ground in Bosnia who were tasked with covertly locating and recording Bosnian Serb military positions and facilities which might be potential targets for NATO air-strikes. The personnel engaged in these tasks were either working for UNPROFOR, NATO, or their own national armed forces. Among those working for UNPROFOR were group -- a group of British soldiers known as JCOs. Several countries had their own soldiers working covertly in Bosnia, and although they reported directly to their national command, they would share information on targets and intelligence with NATO. The witness knows that national elements were providing information used in compiling the target list for NATO air-strikes because he saw such lists. National elements had forward air controllers on the ground in Bosnia as well. These forward air controllers operated both inside and outside of the enclaves in Bosnia and covertly gathered information on potential targets for NATO air-strikes. General Rupert Smith, the UNPROFOR force commander and a general in the British Army was aware that there were forward air controllers on the ground in Bosnia and that they assisted NATO to conduct the air-strikes in Pale in May 1995. The ammunition depot in Pale was an important installation of the Serbs. The Muslims were unable to reach it from any other position. The NATO bombing of that ammunition depot was a significant setback to the Serbs in the war and provided a military advantage to the Muslims. During the time in Bosnia, the Witness KW554, he had frequent contacts with United Nations military observers, UNMOs. Although they were supposed to be unarmed and neutral observers, virtually every UNMO who he encountered in Bosnia thought he was James Bond and tried to do sneaking and peeking. Witness KW554 used them as sources of information. Other national elements also tasked UNMOs to collect information for them from time to time. Witness KW554 would hide in the trunk when the UNMOs took him through military check-points. Although UNMOs were supposed to be unarmed, many of them had weapons. They were like Rambo. When he returned from Bosnia, Witness KW554 undertook a review of highly classified intelligence information concerning the events in Srebrenica in July 1995. He was seeking to determine if there was any information that Radovan Karadzic had been involved in or informed about the executions which had taken place after the fall of Srebrenica. He found no information connecting Dr. Karadzic to those events. He found this significant, because given the level of information in the material he reviewed, had Dr. Karadzic been involved in or informed about the executions, he would have expected it to be reflected in those materials. [Interpretation] That would be a short summary, and I have no questions for the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Witness, as you have noted, your evidence in chief has been admitted in its entirety in writing. Now you will be further cross-examined by the representative of the Office of the Prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. West.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Good morning, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: No, it's 2.20.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Good afternoon, sir.

utterances.speaker: KW554
utterances.text: Good afternoon, ma'am.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Thank you for meeting with me yesterday. One of the questions I neglected to ask you and I'll ask you now is do you speak B/C/S?

utterances.speaker: KW554
utterances.text: No, I don't.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Now, you have a copy of your statement in front of you?

utterances.speaker: KW554
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Okay. If at any time you need to refer to that, you can just go ahead and do that. Just let me know. The first question I want to ask you regards paragraph 14 of your statement, and in that paragraph you indicate that you were present in the former Yugoslavia in May 1995 when the NATO air-strikes were carried out in Pale, but you were not in Pale; correct?

utterances.speaker: KW554
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: And so any information you have about the situation comes second-hand. You didn't observe it yourself; right?

utterances.speaker: KW554
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Nor did any -- did you have any personal conversations with people who were most affected by the events, like the hostages themselves?

utterances.speaker: KW554
utterances.text: No, I did have some conversations with some of the hostages that were -- that were detained.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Okay. So for example, Patrick Rechner, who is the team leader in Pale, you didn't have a conversation with him, though, did you?

utterances.speaker: KW554
utterances.text: No, not at that time, no. I had spoken with him previously though.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: But at the time or any time thereafter, you didn't have any conversation with him in which he related to you exactly what happened during the hostage situation?

utterances.speaker: KW554
utterances.text: No, I didn't.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: And any information that you received about the crisis was not received in realtime, was it?

utterances.speaker: KW554
utterances.text: Could you explain to me what you would mean by realtime?

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: I take it your testimony was admitted in the Ribic case in Canada, and in that case at page 823, in regard this, you said, "I was aware of communications that were going, but once again it's time delayed. It's within maybe hours or a day or whatever, but it's not minute by minute. I'm not watching these transmissions at all." That's what I mean by realtime. The information you received was delayed, was it not?

utterances.speaker: KW554
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: All right. But nonetheless, you make some general comments about the UNMOs in your statement, and I want to look at those to see if those comments have any relevance to the hostage-taking. Now let's look at paragraphs 24 to 27 and those are the paragraphs in which you speak about the reputation of the UNMOs. The basis of your opinion for these comments comes from your interaction with them as sources; is that right?

utterances.speaker: KW554
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: And the UNMOs with whom you used mostly as sources were Canadian UNMOs; correct?

utterances.speaker: KW554
utterances.text: Yes, that would be correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: And so should we take the comments that you make in this statement to be applicable for the most part to the Canadian UNMOs?

utterances.speaker: KW554
utterances.text: For the most part, but I did have contact with other UNMOs from other nationalities.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Okay. But in paragraph 26 -- in paragraph 26, you say: "Although the UNMOs were supposed to be unarmed, many of them had weapons. They were like Rambo." Of what nationality were these particular UNMOs, these armed UNMOs?

utterances.speaker: KW554
utterances.text: Other than the Canadian -- Canadians that I saw, I do not recall the nationalities of them.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: So then should I understand that when you speak about armed UNMOs, you are specifically speaking about Canadian armed UNMOs and no one else?

utterances.speaker: KW554
utterances.text: No, that is not correct. I did see other UNMOs from other nationalities. I don't recall the countries, but they were armed as well.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Well, let me go again to your Ribic testimony at page 717 and you were asked the question were the UNMOs armed, and your answer was: "I think I mentioned that they looked like Rambos, some of them, not all of them. But they were really misguided. They were armed. I wouldn't say all of them, but certainly the ones that I went with. They were the ones that tried to who me where to hide the weapons, some of them. I'm talking about the Canadian ones now specifically." Do you remember saying that testimony that was admitted in the Ribic case?

utterances.speaker: KW554
utterances.text: Yes, I do. I think the point that I was making at that time was about the hiding of the weapons and how to hide them. That was a Canadian to Canadian only thing. I wasn't trying to make the statement that other UNMOs weren't -- or I didn't have contact with other UNMOs. I think when I said the Canadian thing, I was referring specifically to the fact of hiding weapons.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: And the particular UNMOs that you speak about that were armed, were any of them part of the group that was taken hostage in May 1995?

utterances.speaker: KW554
utterances.text: No, not that I'm aware of.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: And in paragraphs 16 through 22, you speak about knowing in a general way about the existence of forward air controllers in Bosnia. Were any of the hostages who were taken into custody in May 1995 some of these forward air controllers of which you speak?

utterances.speaker: KW554
utterances.text: No, not that I'm aware of.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: If we can go to paragraph 10 of your statement. Here you say, and this is talking about the Markale shelling in February 1994, that you heard that there was a photo showing that one of the mortar shells was detonated by being dropped from a window overlooking the market-place. So that's paragraph 10, and there you wrote that you heard about it. Then we go to paragraph 11. In 11 you say -- you're speaking about the same shelling, and you say: " ... a US soldier told me that the Muslims were responsible for the shelling," and he displayed a photograph of a person dropping a mortar shell from a window overlooking the market-place. "I didn't examine the photo." Now, these paragraphs as you can see are inconsistent. What is the right version?

utterances.speaker: KW554
utterances.text: No, I can see how you would -- would say that. I saw the picture from a distance, about the distance between what you and I are standing right now. It was -- I don't know why I said just "I heard," because I did see it. We had a discussion about the picture, but I did not examine it closely, but from what I was told by my source that I was using at the time or the soldier, that it was a picture of the shelling.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Now, you just said that you were at a distance about where we are right now. Would you agree that's about 10 feet?

utterances.speaker: KW554
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: How big was the picture?

utterances.speaker: KW554
utterances.text: Traditional, I guess the 5 by 8 size picture.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: So at a distance of about 10 feet, a 5 by 8 picture, could you see anything at all?

utterances.speaker: KW554
utterances.text: No, because he did display it very quick and flashed it as opposed to holding it still, so I did not see what was on the picture.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: But you would agree that in order for a person dropping a mortar shell from a window, in order for that to have been -- photo to have been taken of that, the photographer would have had to have been reasonably close; right?

utterances.speaker: KW554
utterances.text: Yes, that is absolutely correct, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: And then the photographer and the camera would have had to have survived the explosion that killed about 66 people and wounded over 140. Wouldn't that be correct?

utterances.speaker: KW554
utterances.text: Yes, that would be correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Now, as regards this particular -- the Markale bombing in February 1994, do you remember what you said about it in your Ribic testimony?

utterances.speaker: KW554
utterances.text: No, I don't.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Let me tell you what you said about it, because you didn't comment at all about this -- about this photograph. Instead at page 768 you said you stood in the market-place and you saw the crater that was created, and then you said: "I have stood where the impact of the mortar round in the market was and I have seen the impact on the ground. Being an ex-artillery man, I have somewhat of a knowledge on how artillery rounds or mortars impact." And then on 7 -- the next page you said: "The way that the round impacted to me, and I'm not an expert at this, indicates that it was a fairly vertical trajectory, straight down as opposed to coming in --" you waved your hand diagonally at this point, "which is what you would have expected from Serbian guns because they were on the hills some kilometres away. So the round would come in on a diagonal trajectory. By my terms what I saw didn't appear to be like that." Do you remember saying that?

utterances.speaker: KW554
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Okay. And so you suggested that the crater you saw looked like it should have been a vertical trajectory as opposed to a diagonal trajectory which would -- diagonal would have supported it being fired from perhaps Serb positions. Is that what we should understand?

utterances.speaker: KW554
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: I don't want to be a Pedant and I certainly don't want to give evidence, but you estimated the distance between you at about 10 feet. Well, from where I'm sitting it seems to be considerably more than that, nearer 20 than 10. If it has to be measured, it has to be measured, but the transcript will only show 10 feet, but I don't think that can be right.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour, for those comments, and appreciate your correcting the record as such, and perhaps we'll get back to that, but if we can stay on this for a moment.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: As regards this very issue, the issue of the crater and it being a vertical trajectory or a diagonal trajectory, the Trial Chamber recently heard evidence from a Canadian UNMO, his name was John Russell, who was one of the people who examined the crater itself.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And for the parties' recollection, this was the testimony regarding the garden hose theory.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: And in his statement, Mr. Russell's statement D2364, at paragraph 22, he said this: "I was struck by how steep of an angle that the round must have come in on to clear the large building adjacent to the crater. This led me to believe that the round had come from a location closer to the crater than a round fired from further away." Mr. Witness, is this just another way of saying the same thing that you said in Ribic?

utterances.speaker: KW554
utterances.text: Yes, I believe so.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Mr. President, may we go in private session?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're in open session, Your Honours. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Now, sir, earlier in your testimony I mentioned Patrick Rechner, you said that you had met him once, but that was after the fact; correct?

utterances.speaker: KW554
utterances.text: No. I met him once before in -- in Bosnia. He had stopped into my office and we just had an informal chat.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: All right. My mistake. And also as regards Mr. Ribic, had you ever met him?

utterances.speaker: KW554
utterances.text: No, I did not meet him specifically, although I knew that he was there, but I did not meet him, no. Not until after the fact.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: And your knowledge of what had happened in Pale in May and June of 1995, that knowledge came from people you spoke to; correct?

utterances.speaker: KW554
utterances.text: It would have been from people I spoke to plus from reports that I would have received from national level reports and from other countries as well. It's not just people I would have spoke to in the theatre. It would have also been from reports.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: And as to those sources, did you have a sense as to where the order to take these hostages came from?

utterances.speaker: KW554
utterances.text: No, I didn't.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Sir, I'm going to remind you of your testimony in the Ribic case. It's page 813 to 814 and you were asked: "Is it true that the order to take hostages came from the top level of Serb leadership?" And your answer was: "I received this intelligence information from direct sources. So this is done at a very high level. This is not a local commander in the field gets to make a decision to take hostages." You go on and speak about this more, but in reminding you of that testimony, do you have -- do you have -- what is your position as regards to where the order came from?

utterances.speaker: KW554
utterances.text: I hope I'm not confusing you here. What I'm -- when I refer to that, I don't know where it came from. I don't know exactly where it came from. We like to have exact. I don't know where it came from. When I talked in the Ribic case, what we tried to have a good grasp on was the knowledge of who was giving orders and when the orders were given. So here when I'm talking about levels, I'm specifically speaking about the military. Now when I say it's from higher up, higher up within a military chain of command as in not in a troop or a section level, not a brigade level -- sorry, not a battalion level but back to a brigade level. So I'm referring to the military structure. It certainly had nothing to do with the political side.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. President, I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, do you have any re-examination?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just one question, Excellency.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Witness, a moment ago you were shown an intercept of the conversation between me and Mr. Deronjic through a go-between. Was there anything in that document which hinted at any possible executions? If you'd like us to, we can call it up again. P04618.

utterances.speaker: KW554
utterances.text: Yes, I'd like to just review it just once again if you don't mind.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] P04618, please. The English version, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. I don't see anything in that indicates executions.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Thank you, Witness, for coming here and testifying.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Should we upload witnesses statement paragraph 30 again. I have a couple of questions for you with respect to the paragraph, Mr. Witness. But we'll not broadcast this.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, sir. Questioned by the Court:

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: The second sentence reads like this: "I was seeking to determine if there was any information that Radovan Karadzic had been involved in or informed about the execution which had taken place after the fall of Srebrenica." So my first question is: What kind of execution were you aware of at the time, or what -- what was that execution like that you were aware of that came to know at the time? It was in July, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: KW554
utterances.text: That's correct. At that time, we certainly didn't have the hindsight that we do now, and no, I did not know numbers or didn't know of how many and so forth or the scope. We had known that Srebrenica had fallen and that the -- I can remember recalling that the -- there was reports that the males had been rounded up, but there was certainly no -- there was no absolute evidence at the time that I saw that there was executions other than the reports saying that we had assumed that that's what was going to happen to these people. I just don't recall. I hope that answers your question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Fair enough. My second question is this: You said that if -- you were seeking to determine if there was information that Radovan Karadzic had been involved. Why Mr. Karadzic? What triggered to try to find whether Karadzic was involved in or not? Why not anybody else?

utterances.speaker: KW554
utterances.text: That's -- that's a good question. When -- and I wouldn't say that it wasn't to try and find anybody else. One of the main areas of responsibility that I had when I was deployed in Bosnia was to try to find and figure out the chain of command and who was giving the orders to whom. So when I returned to Ottawa with the BIRT, it was just a natural evolution for me to -- and I was tasked with it, but it was also a personal thing that I wanted to find out at what level. And because of the material I had a chance to review being highly classified, I would have assumed that I would have been able to find out who gave the orders. Just -- not just on Srebrenica but also I was looking at who gave the orders in a general picture so we could formulate a proper chain of command.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. That concludes your evidence, Mr. Witness. On behalf of the Chamber, I'd like to thank you for your coming to The Hague to give it. I also appreciate the kindness of the representatives of the Canadian government, Mr. Fox and Ms. Soliman. We will rise all together. The hearing is adjourned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Thursday, the 17th day of January, 2013, at 9.00 a.m. 21 22 23 24 25
